# The AI search glossary: https://gerris.ai/guides/ai-search-glossary/

AI search has produced more acronyms in three years than SEO produced in twenty. GEO, AEO, AIO, LLMO, AXO, SXO, GPTO, and a dozen more turn up in agency pitches, often for the same work under a different name. This glossary defines each one in plain language, says which describe a real method and which are relabels, and adds the technical terms and metrics that come with them. The definitions are checked against primary sources where one exists, listed at the end.
The short version: almost every acronym here means making a business easy for AI systems to find, understand, verify, and cite. Google's own documentation says there are no additional requirements or special optimizations needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no new machine-readable files or markup. Ask anyone who sells one of these acronyms to name the tasks, the evidence they will collect, and how the result will be measured. The tasks matter; the acronym does not.

## The acronyms

Most of these name the same job: getting a business found, described correctly, and cited by AI systems. The differences are usually in who is selling the label.

**AAIO (agentic AI optimization) and AXO (agentic experience optimization)**
Preparing a website for AI agents that act for a person: comparing options, filling forms, booking, buying. The practical work is old-fashioned: real buttons and links, labeled form fields, prices and stock stated in text, and checkout steps a machine can follow. Accessible sites are already most of the way there.

**AEO (answer engine optimization)**
Work aimed at being the answer an AI assistant, voice assistant, or answer box gives to a question. Gerris has a full guide: What is answer engine optimization? (/guides/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/)

**AI SEO and AISO (AI search optimization)**
Broad labels for SEO adapted to AI search, or for SEO done with AI tools. The phrase covers both meanings in the wild, so it says little until the seller describes the actual tasks.

**AIO**
Used two ways. Some agencies mean AI optimization, an umbrella for all AI visibility work; others mean AI Overviews optimization, earning citations in Google's AI Overviews specifically. When someone sells AIO, the first question is which one.

**ASO (agentic search optimization)**
Optimizing to be found, evaluated, and acted on by AI agents that research, shortlist, and transact on a person's behalf, not only to be cited in an answer. The agent is the visitor: it compares options, checks prices and terms, and completes steps, so the site has to hold up to a reader that never sees the design. The label collides with App Store Optimization, which has used the same three letters for years, so expect confusion until one usage wins.

**AVO (AI visibility optimization)**
Another umbrella label for improving how often and how accurately AI answers mention a brand. Functionally the same work as GEO and AEO.

**GAIO (generative AI optimization) and GSO (generative search optimization)**
Alternate names for GEO, used by agencies that wanted a label of their own.

**GEO (generative engine optimization)**
Making a business easy for generative AI systems to find, understand, verify, and cite. The term comes from a research paper of that name by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues, first posted in November 2023 and accepted to KDD 2024, which reported that some content changes raised visibility in generative engine responses by up to 40 percent. Gerris explains the practice in What is generative engine optimization? (/guides/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/)

**GPTO (ChatGPT optimization)**
GEO aimed at one engine. Optimizing for a single assistant is a weak plan when buyers use several, and the underlying work is the same for all of them.

**LLMO (large language model optimization) and LLM SEO**
Shaping what large language models say about a brand: consistent facts, a clear entity, and outside sources a model will trust. In practice it overlaps GEO almost completely.

**Search everywhere optimization**
The idea that visibility now depends on many platforms at once, including YouTube, Reddit, TikTok, Amazon, and the AI assistants, along with Google. The observation is fair: AI answers draw heavily on forums and video. The label adds no new technique.

**SEO (search engine optimization)**
Making a site crawlable, indexable, and worth ranking in search engines. Every AI label above still depends on it, because AI systems retrieve from search indexes and crawled pages.

**SEO 2.0**
A marketing name for SEO that accounts for AI answers. It describes a sales pitch more than a method.

**SIO (search intent optimization)**
Matching pages to what a searcher is trying to do. This has been a core part of SEO for well over a decade under the name search intent.

**SXO (search experience optimization)**
Combining search visibility with the experience after the click: speed, clarity, and a page that answers the question. With AI answers, part of that experience now happens before any click, in the summary itself.

**VEO (voice engine optimization)**
Optimizing for spoken answers from voice assistants. The work is the same as AEO: short, direct answers in plain language, attached to a clear entity.

## The machinery

These terms describe how AI search actually works. They are worth learning, because they explain what a site can and cannot influence.

**Agentic browser**
A browser with an AI agent built in that can carry out multi-step tasks for its user. OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas and Perplexity's Comet are examples. They read pages through the same structure screen readers use, which is why semantic HTML matters to them.

**Agentic commerce protocols**
The plumbing that lets AI agents transact: presenting products, taking payment, and completing a checkout inside the conversation. Three open protocols divide the work. ACP (Agentic Commerce Protocol), from OpenAI and Stripe, connects an agent to a merchant's existing commerce systems and sits under instant checkout in ChatGPT. AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol), from Google, covers the payment itself, including proof that the buyer authorized the agent to spend. UCP (Universal Commerce Protocol) is an open standard for the whole transaction between agents, storefronts, and payment providers.

**Agentic RAG**
Retrieval run by an AI agent that decides for itself when to search again, which tools to use, and when it has enough to answer. Deep research features in the major assistants work this way.

**AI crawler**
A bot that fetches web pages for an AI company, either to train models or to answer questions live. OpenAI, for example, runs separate bots for each job and treats each robots.txt setting independently: blocking GPTBot (training) does not block OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search).

**AI Overviews and AI Mode**
Google's two generative search surfaces. AI Overviews is the summary at the top of some results pages, the successor to the Search Generative Experience test; AI Mode is the separate conversational search that uses query fan-out. Google says there are no extra requirements to appear in either beyond ordinary SEO, and their traffic is counted in Search Console's regular Performance report under the Web search type.

**AIPREF**
An IETF effort to standardize how publishers declare what AI systems may do with their content, separating training use from search and answer use. The preferences are expressed through robots.txt and related signals, so one statement covers the whole site instead of page-by-page negotiation. This site's robots.txt already carries AIPREF lines.

**Answer engine**
Any system that replies to a question with a written answer instead of a list of links: ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, Claude, and Google's AI Mode among them.

**Chunking**
Splitting a long document into shorter passages so a retrieval system can index and return each one separately. For a website, the lesson is that each section should make sense on its own, with a heading that says what it covers.

**ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, Claude-User, and Claude-Agent**
Anthropic's four user agents. ClaudeBot collects content that may be used for training, Claude-SearchBot improves Claude's search results, Claude-User fetches a page when a person's question needs it, and Claude-Agent identifies the browsers Anthropic hosts for Claude to complete tasks for users. Each can be allowed or blocked separately in robots.txt.

**Crawler economics**
The emerging economics of AI crawling: what a site gives up, and what it gets back, when AI bots fetch its pages. Its parts now have names. Pay-per-crawl arrangements charge AI companies for access that used to be free. The crawl-to-referral ratio counts how much crawling a site absorbs for each visit a crawler sends back. RSL (Really Simple Licensing) is a machine-readable license a publisher attaches to content to state the terms of AI use. Cloudflare's Content Signals Policy is a robots.txt extension for declaring whether content may be used for search, for AI answers, and for training. Web Bot Auth lets an agent sign its requests cryptographically, so a site can verify which agent is actually asking.

**Embedding (vector embedding)**
A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a passage, so a system can find passages close in meaning to a question even when the words differ. Talk of measuring a brand's semantic distance from a prompt describes this math. No website owner can see or set those numbers directly.

**Google-Extended**
A robots.txt product token Google uses to let publishers decide whether crawled content may be used for training Gemini models and for grounding. Google states that it does not affect a site's inclusion in Google Search and is not a ranking signal.

**GraphRAG**
Retrieval over a knowledge graph of entities and relationships instead of, or alongside, similar text passages. Microsoft Research described it in an April 2024 paper by Darren Edge and colleagues: a language model extracts the entities and relationships from a collection, groups closely related entities into communities, summarizes each community, and builds answers from those summaries. It handles questions that span a whole collection or connect several sources better than passage retrieval, and adds little for single-fact lookups. A lighter variant, LazyGraphRAG (November 2024), brought indexing cost down to that of vector retrieval, 0.1 percent of full GraphRAG. It rewards sites whose facts about people, places, and organizations are stated the same way everywhere, because those facts become the nodes.

**Grounding**
Anchoring an AI answer in sources retrieved at the time of the question rather than in training memory alone. Grounded answers are the ones that carry citations, which makes grounding the moment a website can earn a link.

**Grounding queries**
The searches an AI system actually ran while assembling an answer, which often differ from what the user typed. Bing Webmaster Tools now shows a sample of them for pages it cited.

**Hybrid retrieval**
Finding passages two ways at once: keyword matching (the classic method, often BM25) and meaning matching through embeddings, then merging the results. It is why both the exact words buyers use and clear, plain explanations help a page get retrieved.

**llms.txt**
A proposed Markdown file at a site's root that summarizes the site and links its key pages for language models. It is a proposal, and AI companies have not committed to reading it, but it costs little and this site publishes one: gerris.ai/llms.txt (/llms.txt).

**MCP (Model Context Protocol)**
An open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, that lets AI assistants connect to outside tools and data sources in a standard way. For a business, MCP matters when it wants assistants to query its own systems, such as inventory or bookings, directly.

**OAI-SearchBot**
OpenAI's crawler for ChatGPT's search features. OpenAI says blocking it keeps a site out of ChatGPT search answers, though the site can still appear as a navigational link.

**Query fan-out**
Google's own term for how AI Mode works: it breaks a question into subtopics and issues many searches at once on the user's behalf, then writes one answer from the results. Google described it in May 2025. A page can be cited for a subquestion the user never typed.

**RAG (retrieval-augmented generation)**
A design in which a system first retrieves relevant passages from an index, then has a language model write its answer from them, usually with citations. The approach was named in a 2020 research paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues. AI search assistants are RAG systems built on web indexes. Retrieval is the weak point: when the wrong passages come back, the answer is wrong with full confidence, which is why being the clearest, most retrievable source on a question matters more than being one of many.

**Reranker**
A second model that rescores the top passages a retriever found and puts the most relevant first, before the answer is written. Passages that answer the question directly tend to survive reranking.

## Content and authority

These describe what makes a source worth citing. Most are new names for what good publishers and good PR have always done.

**Answer blocks and passage-level optimization**
Writing each section so it stands alone: a heading phrased as the question, and a direct answer in the first sentence or two beneath it. AI systems lift passages, and a passage that needs the paragraph before it to make sense gets skipped.

**Attribute list**
The short set of facts and differentiators a business wants AI answers to repeat about it: what it does, where, for whom, and what sets it apart. Writing one down is useful, because consistency across the web is what lets engines repeat it.

**Brand co-occurrence**
How often a brand's name appears near the topics, places, and descriptions it wants to be known for, on sites other than its own. It is the AI-era name for being mentioned in the right company, which is earned through press, reviews, and community, and cannot be faked at scale without risk.

**Claim layer**
Gerris' name for the structured statements a business publishes about itself so machines can read them directly: entity schema, FAQ markup, llms.txt, and one canonical description of what the business is.

**Entity**
A specific, identifiable thing, such as a person, business, product, or place, that search engines and AI systems track as one item across many sources. Entity-first SEO means making sure every source describes the same entity the same way.

**FAQ markup**
FAQPage structured data. Google deprecated the FAQ rich result and stopped showing it in Search on May 7, 2026, so the markup no longer earns an expanded listing. It still describes a page's questions and answers in a form any machine can read, and the questions themselves remain useful on the visible page.

**Information gain and non-commodity content**
What a page adds that other pages on the topic do not: original data, first-hand experience, a tested method, a named expert. Pages with something new to say have a reason to be cited; pages that restate the consensus do not. Google has described the same quality as content that is original and non-commodity.

**Knowledge graph**
A database of entities and the relationships between them. Google's Knowledge Graph feeds its knowledge panels, and AI systems build similar structures. Knowledge graph alignment means your schema, profiles, and listings all agree.

**LLM seeding**
Deliberately placing a brand's facts and presence in the sources models already trust and retrieve: reference works, community forums, review sites, and best-of lists. Answers are synthesized from a consensus of sources, so the work is getting the brand into that consensus, accurately and in the right company, instead of only publishing on its own site.

**Prompt-to-publish loop**
Researching the questions buyers put to AI assistants and publishing pages that answer them. This is keyword research with longer queries, and it works best when each answer lives on one page instead of many near-duplicates.

## The metrics

Measurement in AI search is young, and every tool measures a sample. These terms are useful when the method behind them is stated.

**AI citation rate**
The share of answers, across a fixed set of questions, that link to or footnote your domain. It only means something when the question set, engines, dates, and location are written down and repeated the same way.

**AI Performance (Bing Webmaster Tools)**
A report Microsoft introduced in public preview on February 10, 2026. It shows how often a site is cited as a source in Microsoft Copilot and in AI-generated summaries in Bing: total citations, the average number of cited pages, per-URL citation counts, and sampled grounding queries. See how to read Bing’s AI Performance report (/guides/bing-ai-performance-report/).

**Citation gap**
The questions, and the sources credited on them, where competitors are cited and your business is absent. Mapped out, the gap is the working plan for closing the distance: which questions are worth answering, and which sources are worth being present in.

**Citation share**
A site's share of all citations for a given grounding query or set of questions: your citations divided by the citations credited to every site for that query. Bing Webmaster Tools' AI Performance report presents citation share in this form. It measures a share of the evidence an answer was built from, which is related to, but not the same as, ranking.

**Cross-model visibility**
How consistently a brand appears across different AI systems, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, and Copilot. Engines draw on different sources, so a brand can be named by one and missing from another.

**Ghost citations**
Citations to a page that never name the brand in the answer text: the source is credited in the footnotes, and the brand itself stays invisible to the reader. The mirror case is a mention with no citation behind it, where the engine names the brand but credits nothing. Both are counted apart from ordinary citations and mentions, because each is visibility that did not fully land.

**Hallucination rate**
How often AI answers state something false about a business: wrong prices, closed locations, invented services. Every wrong fact has a source or a gap behind it, and tracing that source is the start of the fix.

**Mention rate**
How often an AI answer names a brand, with or without a link. Mentions and citations are separate measures: a brand can be named without its site being cited, and a site can be cited for a fact without the brand being recommended.

**Prompt monitoring, prompt panels, and prompt volume**
Tools that run a fixed set of questions through AI assistants on a schedule and record the answers. A prompt panel is that question set; prompt volume is an estimate of how often people ask something similar. Volume figures are modeled estimates, since no AI company publishes query counts the way search engines publish keyword data.

**Recommendation rate and shortlist inclusion**
How often an answer engine not only mentions a business but recommends it, or includes it in the shortlist of candidates it puts forward. A mention says the engine knows the business exists; a recommendation spends the engine's credibility on it. The rate is tracked separately from mention rate because the two move separately.

**Share of model and share of answer**
The AI version of share of voice: how often an assistant names your brand compared with competitors across a set of prompts. Because answers vary from run to run, a single check proves little; repeated, dated runs show the trend.

**Zero-click visibility**
Presence in answers that users read without visiting any website. Rankings and mentions can grow while clicks fall, so reports should track both.

## Which of these names real work?

Three ideas carry the weight. The first is that AI systems retrieve from search indexes and crawled pages, so technical SEO still decides whether a site can be found at all. The second is that answers are assembled from many sources, so the facts on a business's own site, its Google Business Profile, its listings, and the press about it have to agree. The third is that citations go to pages with something worth citing: original evidence, clear answers, and an identifiable author. Every acronym above is a way of packaging some part of those three.
For the measurement side, the guide to how AI answers choose which businesses to name (/guides/how-ai-answers-choose-businesses/) walks through the entity record, the consistency check, and the citability test. For definitions of traditional SEO terms, such as canonical tags, crawl budget, and soft 404s, see the glossaries on christopherabraham.com (https://christopherabraham.com/guides/glossary/) and gerriscorp.com (https://gerriscorp.com/guides/glossary/).

# CV and résumé of Chris Abraham: https://gerris.ai/about/cv/

Christopher James Abraham, Arlington, Virginia. Senior technical SEO and GEO specialist. Building websites since 1994, doing SEO since 1998. Available for remote contract, part-time, and full-time work, Eastern Time.
Download the CV (PDF) LinkedIn Book a 30 minute call
Recruiters and hiring managers: the PDF above is the current version, kept up to date on this page. The summary below is the same record in brief. What recruiters usually ask for is covered here: technical SEO for large and e-commerce sites, crawling and analytics tooling, JavaScript SEO, Core Web Vitals, GEO and AI search visibility across Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and headless and commerce platforms including Salesforce Commerce Cloud and Contentful.

# How do you read Bing’s AI Performance report?: https://gerris.ai/guides/bing-ai-performance-report/

Bing's AI Performance report shows site owners, in Microsoft's own numbers, how often its AI answers cite their pages. It lives in Bing Webmaster Tools, Microsoft introduced it as a public preview on February 10, 2026, and in October 2026 it gained a beta view called Topics Portfolio. This guide explains what each number means, what Microsoft says the numbers do not mean, and how to turn them into work on a site.

## What does the AI Performance report measure?

It measures citations: the times a page from your site is shown as a source in an AI-generated answer. Microsoft says the report covers Microsoft Copilot, AI-generated summaries in Bing, and select partner integrations, which it does not name. Microsoft calls the release an early step toward tooling for generative engine optimization.

## What does each number mean?

**Total Citations**
The total number of citations shown as sources in AI answers during the time frame you pick. Microsoft counts them without indicating where in an answer they appeared or how they were presented.

**Average Cited Pages**
The average number of distinct pages from your site shown as sources per day. Microsoft says it does not indicate ranking, authority, or the role a page played.

**Grounding queries**
The phrases the AI used when it retrieved the content it cited. Microsoft says the data is a sample of overall citation activity.

**Page-level citation activity**
Citation counts for specific URLs on your site over the selected dates, reflecting how often each page is cited, not its importance or placement.

**Visibility trends**
A timeline of how citation activity changes over time across the AI experiences the report covers.

## Why don't grounding queries match my keywords?

A grounding query is the search the AI ran, which is rarely the question a person typed. An assistant breaks a question into smaller searches, the same pattern Google calls query fan-out (/guides/ai-search-glossary/#query-fan-out), and cites whatever answers each piece best. A page about roof repair in Arlington can be cited for a grounding query about permit rules that nobody ever typed into a search box. That makes the list valuable: it shows the subquestions your pages already answer, in the AI's own words, and it is a sample, so read it as evidence of patterns, not a complete log.

## What does Topics Portfolio add?

Topics Portfolio, introduced as a beta on October 13, 2026, groups the grounding queries where your site appears into broader themes, and shows the market around each one:

- Topic size: the approximate total citations across all sites for that theme, a measure of how much AI search demand it carries.
- Sites cited: how many sites appear for the theme's queries, which shows how crowded it is.
- Queries: the approximate number of distinct grounding queries in the theme.
- Opportunity queries: queries where other sites are cited and yours is not, with citation volumes shown as ranges.

Microsoft is plain about the limits: the topic grouping is AI-generated and can be imperfect, the sizes are approximate, branded queries can show up as opportunities, and the figures are meant as directional signals for planning, not a precise ledger. Topics with too little data are not shown at all.

## How should a business read it?

Read it in four passes, month over month, with the same date range each time:

- Which pages are cited, and which are not. Compare the cited pages with the pages you want cited: services, locations, and the canonical statement of what the business is. A blog post cited while the service page is absent is a structure problem, usually fixable.
- What the grounding queries ask. Turn recurring subquestions into headings, and answer each directly in the first sentence under it, so the passage stands on its own.
- Where the opportunities sit. An opportunity query in a crowded topic is a harder win than one in a topic few sites answer. Start where the topic is real and the field is thin.
- Whether the trend moved after the fix. Record the date of every change, then read the timeline against it. A citation count that rises across unrelated pages at once is more likely a change in the engine than in the site.

## What does Microsoft recommend to earn more citations?

Microsoft's own advice is ordinary good publishing: strengthen depth and expertise, use clear headings, tables, and FAQ sections, support claims with examples, data, and cited sources, keep content fresh and accurate, and reduce ambiguity across formats. It also points site owners to IndexNow, so changed pages reach Bing quickly, and local businesses to Bing Places for Business. Bing says it respects robots.txt and other control mechanisms, so a site that blocks Bingbot will not show up here.

## What can't the report tell you?

It covers Microsoft's experiences only. What ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, or Google's AI Overviews say about a business needs its own measurement: a fixed set of buyer questions, run on a schedule, with the answers recorded. Google counts AI Overviews and AI Mode traffic inside the ordinary Performance report in Search Console, with no separate citation view. Bing's report shows Microsoft's citations directly, which makes it a useful calibration point for the rest.

## Frequently asked questions

Is Bing's AI Performance report free?
Yes. It sits inside Bing Webmaster Tools, which is free for any site owner who verifies the site. Microsoft introduced it as a public preview on February 10, 2026.
Does AI Performance show ChatGPT or Google citations?
No. It covers Microsoft Copilot, AI-generated summaries in Bing, and select partner integrations Microsoft does not name. Citations in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, and Google's AI Overviews have to be measured separately, with a fixed set of questions run on a schedule.
Why does my site not show a Topics Portfolio tab?
Microsoft shows it only when a site has enough data, and topics with too little data are left out. Smaller sites may see a shorter list or none at all.
Does a higher citation count mean my page ranks better?
Not by Microsoft's own definitions. Total Citations is counted without placement in the answer, and page-level counts reflect how often a page is cited, not its importance or ranking.

Read next: the guide to how AI answers choose which businesses to name (/guides/how-ai-answers-choose-businesses/), and the AI search glossary (/guides/ai-search-glossary/) for every term used here.

## Sources

- Bing Webmaster Blog: Introducing AI Performance in Bing Webmaster Tools (February 10, 2026) (https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/February-2026/Introducing-AI-Performance-in-Bing-Webmaster-Tools-Public-Preview)
- Bing Webmaster Blog: Introducing Topics Portfolio (Beta) in AI Performance (October 13, 2026) (https://blogs.bing.com/webmaster/2026/10/introducing-topics-portfolio-beta-in-ai-performance/)
- Google Search Central: AI features and your website (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)

# GitHub Pages with Jekyll or plain HTML: https://gerris.ai/guides/jekyll-or-plain-html/

GitHub Pages serves finished HTML files, and there are two ways to produce them: let Jekyll assemble the pages from Markdown and templates, or write the HTML yourself, by hand or with your own build script. Gerris runs both. hillmole.com, Chris Abraham's serialized novel, is a Jekyll site with 309 entries moved from Movable Type in October 2026. gerris.ai, christopherabraham.com, gerriscorp.com, chrisabraham.net, and thechrisabrahamshow.com are plain HTML. Chris built every one of them and maintains them all, which settles the first question people ask: the work is the same either way—writing and editing text files, then publishing. The choice depends on the site.

## What does Jekyll do on GitHub Pages?

Jekyll is a static site generator, and GitHub runs it on every Pages site published from a branch unless you tell it not to. You write each page or post as Markdown with a block of YAML front matter at the top: title, date, layout, and any other values. Jekyll pours that content into layouts written in Liquid, its templating language, and writes the finished HTML. A _config.yml file holds the site's settings, including front matter defaults: a rule that every file of one type, in one path, gets the same values unless the file says otherwise.
GitHub's build runs Jekyll 3.10 through the github-pages gem, with a fixed list of supported plugins. That list includes jekyll-feed, jekyll-sitemap, jekyll-seo-tag, and jekyll-redirect-from, and GitHub Pages will not run a plugin outside it. A site that needs anything else builds through a custom GitHub Actions workflow, which can deploy the output of any static site generator.

## What is a plain HTML site on GitHub Pages?

A plain HTML site is the finished pages committed to the repository, with a file named .nojekyll in the root so GitHub publishes them untouched. GitHub added that file in 2009 for sites whose files or folders start with an underscore, which Jekyll otherwise treats as its own and leaves out. The pages can be written by hand, as on gerris.ai, or generated by a script you control. christopherabraham.com and gerriscorp.com are built by a Python script that writes every page, the sitemap, the feeds, and llms.txt from source files, and refuses to finish if a title runs long or two pages repeat each other. thechrisabrahamshow.com rebuilds itself every morning from its podcast feed, in a scheduled GitHub Actions job.

## What is each approach good at?

- Jekyll suits a site that grows by adding writing: a blog, a serialized book, an archive, documentation. A new post is one Markdown file, and a change to one layout changes every page. It also handles a migration well. Hill Mole's Movable Type archive pages became a Jekyll collection, and one front matter default keeps every one of them out of the sitemap and marked noindex while their old URLs still answer.
- Plain HTML suits a site where every page is deliberate: a business site, a service catalog, a set of guides. Nothing is assembled at request time or at GitHub's build, so what is in the repository is exactly what visitors and crawlers receive. A custom build script can enforce rules Jekyll has no plugin for, such as unique titles, length limits on descriptions, and a check against phrasing borrowed from a sibling site.

## How do they compare?

QuestionJekyll on GitHub PagesPlain HTML

Where pages are builtGitHub's build, from Markdown and Liquid layoutsYour own editor, script, or workflow
Adding a pageOne Markdown file with front matterOne finished page, or one source file your script expands
Changing every pageEdit one layoutEdit the template in your script, or every file by hand
Plugins and extensionsGitHub's supported list only, unless you build with ActionsAnything your own build can do
Files starting with an underscoreSkipped unless included in _config.ymlPublished as they are, with .nojekyll
Builds per hourA soft limit of 10 on GitHub's buildNo limit when published through your own Actions workflow

The rest of GitHub's limits are the same either way: a published site no larger than 1 GB, a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB a month, and deployments that time out after 10 minutes.

## How does the work compare in practice?

Working in either kind of repository means following its conventions. In a Jekyll site the conventions are fixed and public: where layouts live, what front matter means, which plugins exist. In a plain HTML site with a build script, the conventions are whatever the script enforces, and the script's checks become the checklist every change is run against. Either way the work is writing text files and running a build. Hill Mole's move from Movable Type to Jekyll and the plain HTML builds of the other five sites are all Chris's own work, and he decides what each site says.
The difference that matters is where the rules live. Jekyll carries its rules in the framework, so anyone who picks up the repository already knows most of them. A custom build carries its rules in the script and a written briefing, so the briefing has to be kept current, or the next round of changes will quietly undo the last one's work.

## Which should you choose?

Choose Jekyll when the site is mostly writing that keeps arriving, when you want to add pages in Markdown without touching HTML, or when you are moving a blog off a platform such as Movable Type or WordPress and need its old URLs kept. Choose plain HTML when the site is a fixed set of pages that must each say something exact, when you want a build that checks every page before it publishes, or when the site has to pass through no processing at all. For AI search, both publish the same thing a crawler reads, and the work that earns citations is the same: clear titles, structured data, a sitemap, an llms.txt, and pages that answer questions directly.
One limit applies to both. GitHub's terms say Pages is not intended or allowed for running an online business, an e-commerce site, or any site primarily directed at commercial transactions, and it should never carry passwords or card numbers. A brochure site, a practice, a portfolio, a book, or a publication fits. A store with a checkout belongs on a platform built for it.

## Frequently asked questions

Does GitHub Pages use Jekyll by default?
Yes, for a site published from a branch. GitHub runs its own Jekyll build on the repository unless a file named .nojekyll sits in the root, or the site is published through a custom GitHub Actions workflow.
What does a .nojekyll file do?
It tells GitHub Pages to skip Jekyll and publish the files exactly as they are. GitHub added it in 2009 for sites whose files or folders start with an underscore, which Jekyll treats as its own and does not copy.
What skills does each approach take?
Jekyll takes Markdown and YAML front matter for the pages, with the layouts written once in Liquid and reused. Plain HTML takes HTML itself, page by page, or a build script you write and maintain. Gerris runs one Jekyll site and five plain HTML sites, all built and kept by Chris, and the working skills are the same in both: writing clean text files, keeping titles and descriptions honest, and checking the output before it publishes.
Which is better for SEO, Jekyll or plain HTML?
Neither, by itself. Both publish finished HTML that every crawler reads. What decides search and AI visibility is what the build puts in the pages: titles, descriptions, schema, sitemaps, and what it refuses to publish.
Can I run an online store on GitHub Pages?
No. GitHub's terms say Pages is not intended or allowed for running an online business or an e-commerce site, or for sending passwords or card numbers. Brochure sites, guides, portfolios, and archives fit; checkouts belong on a platform built for them.

Read next: GitHub Pages websites built by Gerris (/services/github-pages-websites/), and the AI search glossary (/guides/ai-search-glossary/) for the terms that decide what an answer engine does with the pages.

# Guide: Why is my website not indexed by Google?: https://gerris.ai/guides/why-is-my-website-not-indexed/

Home › Guides › Why is my website not indexed by Google?
Why is my website not indexed by Google?
A page that is not in Google's index does not exist for search. It cannot rank, it cannot appear in AI Overviews, and the answer engines that draw on search indexes cannot cite it. Indexing is the floor under every other kind of visibility, and it is the first thing Gerris checks on any site, because the most common reason a business is invisible is also the plainest one: the pages were never admitted to the index in the first place. This guide covers why pages get left out, how to check yours, and the order of fixes that gets them in. The repair work itself is on the services page.
What does it mean for a page to be indexed?
Google's system runs in three stages. A crawler fetches the page. The index stores what the crawler found, organized so it can be retrieved. Serving answers queries from the index, not from the live web. A page can clear the first stage and fail the second: Google crawled it, read it, and decided to leave it out. Search Console reports this state in so many words, "Crawled - currently not indexed," and it is a decision, not an error. The page was weighed as a candidate for the index and the index declined it, usually because the same content exists elsewhere in a stronger form, or because the page gives the index too little that is new to store.
The second failure state is "Discovered - currently not indexed." Google knows the URL exists, from a sitemap or a link, and has not yet spent a crawl on it. On a small site this clears on its own. On a site that publishes faster than it earns attention, the discovered queue grows, and the pages at the back of it can wait months.
What blocks a page from being indexed at all?
Some pages never reach the decision stage because an instruction stops them first. The blocks, in the order the desk finds them:
A noindex instruction: a meta tag or an X-Robots-Tag header telling every engine to leave the page out. Development sites ship with it on; migrations carry it live by accident.
A robots.txt block: the crawler is forbidden to fetch the page, so Google can only list a bare URL with no content, or drop it entirely.
A canonical tag pointing elsewhere: the page declares another URL the real version of itself, and the index keeps the other one.
Server and redirect failures: the page returns an error, a redirect chain that dies, or a soft 404, a page that says "not found" in its text while returning a success code.
Orphan pages: no internal link leads to the page, so the crawler has no path to it and the index has no signal that the site itself values it.
Login walls and rendering failures: the content sits behind a sign-in, or it only exists after scripts run that the crawler could not complete.
Every item on that list is mechanical, and every one is fixable. Blocks like these are why Gerris treats indexing as a repair trade before it treats it as a strategy question.
Why does Google index a page and then drop it?
Because the index is a store with standards, not an archive of everything crawled. Pages fall out when the store re-weighs them: the content thinned after an edit, a stronger page on the same site started answering the same query, the page's links disappeared in a redesign, or the site as a whole lost the crawl attention that kept marginal pages in. Duplicate content is the steady cause. When three pages say the same thing in nearly the same words, the index keeps the one it judges the original and releases the other two, and the released pages are usually the ones the business expected to rank.
How do you check whether your pages are indexed?
Four checks, in order. First, the site search: type site:yourdomain.com into Google and compare the count against the number of pages you publish. It is rough and it is fast. Second, the Page indexing report in Search Console, which lists every URL Google knows about on your site and the exact reason each excluded page was excluded. Third, the URL Inspection tool on your money pages one at a time: it reports the page's index state, its canonical as Google sees it, and when it was last crawled. Fourth, your sitemap: a sitemap that lists URLs the index has dropped, or omits the pages you care about, is telling you where the disagreement lives. The desk runs these four before it recommends anything, because the fix for a blocked page and the fix for a declined page are different jobs.
How do you get a page indexed?
Remove the block first, if there is one: lift the noindex, open the robots.txt rule, repair the canonical, fix the error. Then give the crawler a path and a reason. Link the page from indexed pages that matter, in the body text, with anchor text that says what the page is. List it in the sitemap. Make the page worth storing: a clear statement of its subject in the words buyers search, enough substance that the index gains something by keeping it, and no near-twin elsewhere on the site competing for the same slot. Request indexing in Search Console once the page is fixed, as a notification, not a lever. Then wait and verify in the same reports you checked at the start. Indexing earned this way holds. Indexing begged for, on a page that is still blocked or still a duplicate, does not.
That sequence, run across a whole site, is the indexing repair on the Gerris services page: a one-problem repair is $500 flat, and a whole-site repair is $750 flat, each scoped in writing before it begins.
Frequently asked questions
How long does it take Google to index a new page?
On an established site with internal links pointing at it, a new page is usually crawled within days and indexed within a week or two. On a new site, or a page with no links and no sitemap entry, the same page can wait months. The difference is rarely the page. It is the crawl attention the site has earned and the paths the site gives the crawler.
Does requesting indexing in Search Console guarantee a page gets indexed?
No. Request indexing asks for a crawl. It does not overrule a noindex tag, a robots.txt block, a canonical pointing elsewhere, or Google's judgment that the page duplicates a stronger one. Fix the cause first, then request. The request is the last step of a repair, not a substitute for one.
Why was my page dropped from the index?
The usual causes are duplication, thinning, and neglect: another page began answering the same query better, an edit removed the substance the index was storing, or a redesign removed the internal links that kept the page in circulation. Search Console's Page indexing report names the state Google put the page in, and that state is where the repair starts.
How much does it cost to fix indexing problems?
Gerris prices indexing repair in the open. A one-problem repair is $500 flat and a whole-site repair is $750 flat, each scoped in writing before work begins. The diagnosis comes from Search Console's own reports, so the scope names the exact pages and the exact blocks before anyone pays for the fix.

# Guide: What is llms.txt, and does your business need one?: https://gerris.ai/guides/what-is-llms-txt/

Home › Guides › What is llms.txt, and does your business need one?
What is llms.txt, and does your business need one?
llms.txt is a plain-text file at the root of a website that tells language models what the site is, in the site's own words. It sits beside robots.txt and the sitemap, in the layer of a site that exists to instruct machines. Where robots.txt tells crawlers where they may go and the sitemap lists every URL, llms.txt does a different job: it states the business's name, what it sells, where it works, and which pages matter, in clean markdown that a language model can read in one pass. Gerris publishes one for this site, linked in the footer of every page, and builds one into every site it delivers. This guide explains what the file is, what goes in it, and what it honestly can and cannot do.
Where did llms.txt come from?
The format was proposed in 2024 by Jeremy Howard as a standard location and structure for information meant for large language models. The problem it answers is real: a modern web page arrives at a model wrapped in navigation, scripts, and layout markup, and the model spends its limited attention digging the facts out of the furniture. A plain markdown file removes the digging. The proposal is a convention, not a law of the web. No engine is required to read the file, and adoption is voluntary on both sides, which is exactly the state robots.txt was in when it became universal.
What goes in an llms.txt file?
The structure is short and fixed. The file opens with the business's name as a heading. Under it, a summary in blockquote form: one short paragraph stating what the business is, what it sells, where it works, and how to reach it, written the way the business would state it on the record. Then come sections of links, the pages that matter, each with a one-line description of what the page says. A key facts section closes the file: prices, service areas, credentials, founding facts, the statements the business most needs repeated correctly. This site's llms.txt carries its prices and its audit scope as key facts, because those are the statements buyers ask engines about and the ones engines most often get wrong from scattered pages.
The discipline is selection. The file is a summary, not a copy of the site. A business that pastes forty pages into it has built a second website in a worse format. Ten to twenty links, the facts that decide purchases, nothing else.
What is llms-full.txt?
The companion convention. Where llms.txt links to the pages that matter, llms-full.txt contains the full text of those pages in one markdown document, so a model or an agent can take in the whole record in a single fetch without crawling page by page. Gerris publishes both. The summary file serves a quick lookup; the full file serves a deep one, an agent researching a vendor, a model assembling a record it intends to rely on. Keeping the two in step is maintenance, the same kind a sitemap needs, and it belongs to whoever maintains the site.
Do AI engines actually read llms.txt?
Server logs settle part of this: AI crawlers and agents fetch the file, on this site and on client sites, and fetch it early in a visit, before the deep pages. What no engine has promised is a ranking or a citation in exchange for having one. The honest claim is narrower and stronger. The summary of your business gets written whether you take part or not, assembled from whatever the engines find. llms.txt is the one place where that summary is stated by you, in full sentences, in a form built for the reader who will repeat it. A business that declines to state its own record is leaving the stating to directories, reviews, and competitors' comparisons.
How do you keep an llms.txt file true?
The same way you keep a sitemap true: by tying it to the site's one set of facts and updating it in the same pass as the pages. When a price changes, the price changes on the services page, in the schema, and in the key facts section of llms.txt, in one edit, from one source. When a page is retired, its link leaves the file. The failure mode to avoid is the orphaned file, written once at launch and never touched again, still stating the old phone number and the old service area two years later in the business's own voice. An engine that finds the file and the site disagreeing believes the disagreement is real and reports both versions, which is worse than the file never existing. Gerris treats the machine layer, robots.txt, sitemap, schema, llms.txt, as one document in four formats, and maintains it that way.
How is llms.txt different from robots.txt and a sitemap?
Each file in the machine layer answers a different question. Robots.txt answers where crawlers may go, and the crawler guide covers the decisions it carries. The sitemap answers what URLs exist. Schema answers what the facts on a page mean, in structured form, and the schema guide covers that layer. llms.txt answers the question none of the others ask: what is this business, stated plainly, by itself. The four files agree or the record blurs, which is why Gerris writes them as one layer, from one set of facts.
Frequently asked questions
Does having an llms.txt file improve my rankings?
No engine has promised that, and any vendor who guarantees it is inventing the promise. What the file does is verifiable from your own server logs: AI crawlers fetch it, and they fetch the summary you wrote instead of assembling one from scattered pages. It is a statement of record, cheap to publish and cheap to keep correct, not a ranking lever.
Where does the llms.txt file live?
At the root of the domain, at yourdomain.com/llms.txt, in plain text with markdown formatting. One file per site. The companion full-text version lives beside it at /llms-full.txt. Both are linked from this site's footer if you want to read a working example before writing yours.
What should a small business put in its llms.txt?
The name of the business, a one-paragraph statement of what it sells and where, links to the homepage, the services pages, and the about page with one-line descriptions, and a key facts section: service area, prices where they are published, credentials, phone, and email. If a fact decides whether a buyer calls, it belongs in the file.
Who writes and maintains llms.txt?
Whoever maintains the website, working from the same facts the site states. Gerris writes the file as part of every site build and updates it when prices, services, or facts change, because a stale llms.txt is worse than none: it states the old record in the business's own voice, and the engines will believe it.

# Guide: What schema markup do AI answer engines actually use?: https://gerris.ai/guides/schema-markup-for-ai-search/

Home › Guides › What schema markup do AI answer engines actually use?
What schema markup do AI answer engines actually use?
Schema markup is a statement of a page's facts in a form machines read directly, and answer engines use it to resolve, verify, and quote the businesses they name. A page of prose makes an engine infer: this string of words is a price, that one is a service area, this person runs the business. Schema removes the inference. In JSON-LD, the format Google recommends and this site uses, the page declares its facts as labeled data: the business's name, its category, its services, its prices, its people, each under its own field name. This guide covers the schema types that matter for AI search, what the markup actually does inside an answer, and the point where it stops working.
Which schema types matter for AI answers?
The working set is short, and every type on it states a fact buyers ask about:
Organization and LocalBusiness: the entity itself. Name, category, address, phone, service area, hours, and sameAs links to the business's profiles, which tell the engine that this website, this Google Business Profile, and this LinkedIn page are one entity, not three similar ones.
Service: each service the business sells, named in the category language buyers search, with the provider tied back to the entity.
Product and Offer: what is sold and at what price. A published price in schema is a fact an engine can quote with confidence, and prices are the facts buyers ask for most.
FAQPage: questions and answers in the buyers' own words, marked as questions and answers, ready to be lifted into a response.
Article: authorship, dates, and the publisher behind a piece of writing, which lets an engine attribute a claim to a named, accountable source.
Person: the people behind the business, their roles and credentials, tied to the organization they run.
BreadcrumbList and WebSite: the structure of the site itself, which pages sit under which, so a retrieved page arrives with its context attached.
Everything past this set is decoration for most businesses. A schema type that states no fact a buyer asks about earns nothing.
What does schema do inside an AI answer?
Recall the sequence from the guide on how AI answers choose businesses: retrieval, resolution, corroboration, composition. Schema works at the middle two stages. At resolution, entity schema with sameAs links settles which mentions belong to the same business, so a review, a listing, and a homepage assemble into one record instead of three partial ones. At corroboration, structured facts are cheap to compare across sources: a price stated in schema on your site and the same price stated on a directory listing corroborate each other in a way two paragraphs of marketing prose do not. The engine names and quotes the records it could settle. Schema is how a business files its facts in the form the settling is done in.
Where does schema stop working?
At the visible page. Schema that contradicts the text a visitor can read is discounted, and schema that invents facts the page does not state, services the business does not offer, reviews it does not have, prices it does not charge, is treated as a false filing, because that is what it is. The markup is a statement of the page's facts, not a second, better page hidden from humans. The desk's rule when writing it: every value in the JSON-LD must be findable in the visible text of the page it sits on. A business that follows that rule gets the full benefit of the format. A business that games it gets the markup ignored and, in Google's system, risks a structured data penalty on top.
How do you check the schema on your own site?
View the source of a money page and search it for application/ld+json; most business sites have either none or a plugin's generic minimum. Run the URL through Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema Markup Validator, which report errors and, more usefully, show you exactly which facts the machines extracted. Then read the extraction against the page. The test that matters is not whether the markup validates. It is whether the extracted record is the record you would state yourself: right category, right services, right prices, right people. The AI Visibility Audit includes that read, because schema errors are entity errors, and entity errors are what keep businesses out of answers.
One maintenance warning belongs in every schema conversation: the markup drifts. A redesign rebuilds the pages and drops the JSON-LD blocks. A plugin update replaces careful Service entries with a generic WebPage statement. A price changes in the visible text and stays old in the Offer. Each drift reopens the inference the markup was written to close, and it reopens silently, because the page looks identical to a human visitor. The check above takes minutes per page and belongs on the schedule after every site change, the same discipline the llms.txt guide prescribes for the machine layer as a whole: one set of facts, stated the same way, in every format the machines read.
Frequently asked questions
Does schema markup guarantee my business gets cited in AI answers?
No. Schema makes your facts easier to resolve, verify, and quote, and engines prefer sources that cost them the least doubt. It does not compel a citation. The businesses that get cited combine settled schema with consistent facts across their profiles and pages that answer buyer questions in quotable form. Schema is the filing system, not the whole record.
Should schema be written in JSON-LD or microdata?
JSON-LD. It is the format Google recommends, it sits in one block that can be audited at a glance, and it can be updated without touching the visible markup of the page. Microdata and RDFa scatter the same statements through the HTML, where they drift out of step with the text every time the page is edited.
Can schema markup hurt my site?
Yes, when it lies. Markup that states facts the visible page does not, fabricated reviews, invented prices, services the business does not offer, is treated as a false statement: engines discount it, and Google can apply a manual action against the site's structured data. Schema written strictly from the visible page carries no such risk.
What schema does a small business site need first?
Organization or LocalBusiness with sameAs links, one Service entry per service sold, FAQPage on pages that answer buyer questions, and Article on anything published under a byline. That set states who you are, what you sell, and what buyers ask, which is the record the answer engines assemble.

# Guide: Which AI crawlers should your robots.txt allow?: https://gerris.ai/guides/which-ai-crawlers-should-you-allow/

Home › Guides › Which AI crawlers should your robots.txt allow?
Which AI crawlers should your robots.txt allow?
The AI crawlers are not one crawler, and blocking them as a class is how a business deletes itself from AI search while believing it only declined training. Each engine company sends several bots with different jobs. Some build the search indexes the answers are retrieved from. Some fetch a page at the moment a user asks. Some collect material to train future models. A robots.txt rule written against the company's name blocks all of its bots at once, the training crawler and the search crawler together, and the business vanishes from that engine's answers for a reason it never chose. This guide names the crawlers, separates the jobs, and states the settings Gerris recommends and runs on this site.
What are the three jobs AI crawlers do?
Search crawlers build and refresh the indexes that answers are retrieved from: OpenAI's OAI-SearchBot, Perplexity's PerplexityBot, Anthropic's Claude-SearchBot, and Googlebot and Bingbot behind them. User-triggered fetchers retrieve a page live, when a person asks the engine to look at it: ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, Perplexity-User. Training crawlers collect pages to train future models: OpenAI's GPTBot, Anthropic's ClaudeBot, Meta's Meta-ExternalAgent, Apple's Applebot-Extended, Common Crawl's CCBot, ByteDance's Bytespider. The jobs matter because the consequences of blocking them are opposite. Block a training crawler and your pages stay out of a future model's training set while your search visibility is untouched. Block a search crawler and your pages leave the index the answers are built from.
Which crawlers does a business need to allow?
The search and fetching crawlers, if the business wants to be found by the engines' users: OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User for ChatGPT, PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User for Perplexity, Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User for Claude, and Googlebot and Bingbot, which feed Google's and Microsoft's answers as they always fed their results pages. The training crawlers are the owner's genuine choice. Gerris allows them on this site, on the reasoning that a business selling visibility gains more from being known by the models than it loses from being read by them, and states that as a recommendation, not a rule. What the desk advises against, for any business that sells to people who ask engines questions, is the blanket block: every AI user agent disallowed, usually installed by a security plugin or a host's default, discovered months later when the owner asks why ChatGPT has never heard of them.
Can you block AI Overviews without blocking Google Search?
No. AI Overviews are built from Google's search index and crawled by Googlebot, the same crawler behind the ordinary results. A business that blocks Googlebot leaves Google Search entirely. The separate control, Google-Extended, governs whether Google may use crawled content for Gemini model training and grounding; it does not remove a site from AI Overviews or AI Mode. Vendors who sell a switch that keeps the ranking and drops the AI answer are selling a switch that does not exist. The choice Google actually offers is the old one: be in the index, on the record, or be out of it.
Where else do AI crawlers get blocked?
Robots.txt is only the written layer. Firewalls and content delivery networks block bots by default rules their owners never see, and a host migration can carry a block forward for years. The check is threefold. Read your robots.txt at yourdomain.com/robots.txt and look for the AI user agents by name. Read your server or CDN logs for the crawlers above and note whether they receive your pages or a 403. Then ask the engines questions about your business and see whether the answers know your site exists, which is the test the AI Visibility Audit runs formally. A block at any layer produces the same absence, and the absence looks, from the owner's chair, exactly like being ignored by the engines. The selection guide lists blocked crawlers first among the reasons answers skip a business, because in the audits it is the first one found.
What settings does Gerris recommend?
Allow the search crawlers and the user-triggered fetchers by name. Decide the training crawlers deliberately, by name, knowing which job each one does. Never let a plugin, a host, or a firewall default make the decision unrecorded. And re-check the file after every migration, redesign, or security change, because robots.txt is the file most often overwritten by people who did not know what was in it. The whole review takes an hour on most sites, and it is the cheapest visibility a business can recover: the pages already exist, the engines are already crawling, and the only thing standing between them is a text file.
Keep the evidence while you are at it. Save a copy of the robots.txt you replaced, with the date, and note which agents the new file allows and refuses. When visibility moves afterward, that note is how you know what moved it. Crawler settings are a standing decision of the business, like its prices, and they belong in the same kind of record: written down, dated, and owned by someone who can explain them.
Frequently asked questions
Does blocking GPTBot keep my business out of ChatGPT's answers?
No. GPTBot is OpenAI's training crawler. ChatGPT's search answers are built from OAI-SearchBot's index and from pages fetched live by ChatGPT-User. Blocking GPTBot alone leaves your search visibility intact. Blocking all three OpenAI agents removes you from ChatGPT's answers, which is the outcome businesses usually did not intend when they blocked the training bot.
Does allowing AI crawlers mean my content will be used for training?
It depends on the crawler, which is why the names matter. The search crawlers index your pages so answers can cite them; the training crawlers, GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Meta-ExternalAgent, Applebot-Extended, CCBot, and their peers, collect for model training. Robots.txt lets you allow the first group and refuse the second, agent by agent, and the settings should state the decision for each.
Why does my site block AI crawlers when I never set that?
Defaults. Security plugins ship with bot-blocking rules, hosts enable them during migrations, and CDN bot-management products classify new crawlers as threats until told otherwise. The block is rarely a decision anyone remembers making. It is found by reading the robots.txt file and the crawl logs, which is why the check belongs in every site audit.
Should a business block Bytespider and the aggressive crawlers?
A crawler that ignores robots.txt, hammers a small server, or serves no search product the business's buyers use is a cost with no return, and blocking it at the firewall is ordinary site management. That decision is about load and conduct, made crawler by crawler. It is different from blocking the named search crawlers of the engines your buyers ask questions on, which is a decision about whether to exist in their answers.

# Guide: How do reviews affect what AI answers say about your business?: https://gerris.ai/guides/how-do-reviews-affect-ai-answers/

Home › Guides › How do reviews affect what AI answers say about your business?
How do reviews affect what AI answers say about your business?
Reviews are the loudest third-party voice in your business's record, and AI answers repeat them. When a buyer asks an engine whether a business is good, the engine does not interview your customers. It reads the reviews strangers already wrote, on the platforms it can crawl, and summarizes them: the average rating, the services reviewers name, the complaints that recur, the praise that repeats. A business with twelve reviews from 2021 is described from twelve reviews from 2021. This guide covers what the engines take from reviews, which reviews they can reach, and how a business improves the review record honestly.
What do AI engines take from reviews?
Three things. The rating, as a number an answer can state outright: businesses are introduced with their stars attached, and a 3.8 travels with the name the way a price does. The themes, extracted from the text across many reviews: punctual, expensive, thorough, hard to reach, whatever the reviewers collectively say most often becomes the answer's description of the business's character. And the specifics: a review that names a service, a neighborhood, and an outcome is evidence about what the business does and where it does it, and engines quote specifics when a buyer asks a narrow question. A review that says "great service" contributes a rating point and nothing else. A review that says what was done, for whom, and how it ended contributes facts.
Which review platforms do the engines read?
The ones they can crawl and attribute to your entity: Google reviews, Yelp, TripAdvisor in its trades, the Better Business Bureau, and the industry platforms a trade runs on, the legal directories, the home-services marketplaces, the healthcare rating sites. Attribution is the quiet condition. Reviews attached to a duplicate or misnamed profile describe a business the engine may not connect to you, which is one more reason the entity record in the entity SEO guide matters: the reviews have to resolve to the same business as the website before they count as your evidence. Reviews on a platform that blocks crawlers exist for human visitors and are largely absent from the answers.
Why do old reviews describe your business in new answers?
Because the answer is assembled from the record that exists, and a thin record has no newer material to outweigh the old. Twelve reviews written under a previous owner, at old prices, for a service you no longer offer, are still the whole file if nothing has been added since. Engines weigh volume and recency the way a reader does: a steady run of recent reviews describing the current business displaces the stale file; a stale file standing alone is quoted as the present. This is the same mechanism as the wrong-facts problem in the correction guide, with reviews as the source that will not update itself.
How do you improve the review record honestly?
Ask every customer, at the end of the job, in person and in one follow-up message, with a direct link to the profile. Make the asking part of the work, not a campaign run twice a year, because recency is part of the evidence. Ask for the specifics without scripting them: a customer prompted to say what was done and how it went writes the kind of review an engine can use, and a customer handed a script writes one platforms can flag. Respond to reviews as the owner, briefly and factually; the responses are part of the record the engines read, and a calm factual response to a complaint is evidence about the business too. Then fix, on your own pages, the facts reviewers keep getting wrong, because a wrong fact repeated across twenty reviews started somewhere, and it usually started with a stale page or listing of yours.
Two practices sit outside the honest set and stay there. Buying reviews, or offering anything of value in exchange for them, violates the platforms' rules and consumer law, and the manufactured pattern is legible to the same systems that read the genuine one. Gating, asking only the customers expected to be happy, is the same violation in a quieter coat. The record an engine trusts is the record that was not arranged.
Frequently asked questions
Do star ratings appear in AI answers?
Yes. Ratings are among the facts answers state most directly, usually attached to the business's name in a recommendation, because the rating is a settled, crawlable number the engine can quote without interpretation. The themes from the review text travel with it: the answer that gives your stars often gives the reviewers' summary of your character in the same breath.
How many reviews does a business need before AI answers notice?
There is no published threshold, and the count matters less than the coverage. A business with forty recent reviews across two platforms has a record an engine can summarize with confidence. A business with six reviews, however glowing, has anecdotes. The working goal is a steady flow on the platforms your buyers and the engines actually read, maintained as part of the job.
Should the owner respond to reviews?
Yes, briefly and factually. Responses are read as part of the record: they show the business operating, and a factual response can correct a wrong date, a wrong service, or a case of mistaken identity in the one place the correction sits beside the claim forever. Arguing with reviewers does the opposite work in the same permanent position.
Can fake reviews improve what AI answers say?
They can change it briefly and damage it durably. Platforms detect and remove manufactured reviews, regulators treat bought reviews as deceptive marketing, and an engine summarizing a profile that later gets purged repeats the purge as absence. Gerris does not buy, write, or arrange reviews for clients, and treats a competitor's suspicious profile as a fact to note in an audit, never a tactic to copy.

# Guide: How do you fix wrong information about your business in AI answers?: https://gerris.ai/guides/how-to-fix-wrong-information-in-ai-answers/

Home › Guides › How do you fix wrong information about your business in AI answers?
How do you fix wrong information about your business in AI answers?
A wrong fact in an AI answer is a quotation, and the way to correct a quotation is to correct what it quotes. The old address, the retired service, the price from three years ago: the engine took each one from a source it found, a listing, a directory, a review, an old page of yours, and it will keep taking it from there until the sources change. Owners write to the engine companies asking for a correction desk that does not exist. This guide gives the sequence that works: record the error exactly, trace it to its sources, fix the fact at every source, state the true fact quotably, and re-test until the answer moves.
Where does the wrong fact come from?
Almost always from the public record, in one of four places. Your own site, where a stale page, an old PDF, or a forgotten location page still states the fact. Your profiles and listings, where the fact was entered once and never revisited. Third-party pages, directories, articles, and reviews that repeat the fact and cannot be edited by you. And the model's own memory, where a fact learned in training is repeated without any live source at all. The first three are retrieval errors, fixed at the source. The fourth is slower, and the honest guide says so: a fact held in model memory changes when the corrected record is consistent enough, in enough places, for long enough that the next training run learns the new version. Retrieval is where to start, because most wrong facts in answers with citations are retrieval, and the citation names the source for you.
Step one: record the error exactly
Write down the question you asked, in the words you asked it, the engine, the date, and the wrong claim as stated. Screenshot it. An error that cannot be reproduced cannot be verified as fixed, and answers vary between runs, so the record is what separates a correction from a hope. The measurement guide sets out the observation discipline in full. Do this for every engine that serves your buyers, because the four engines draw on different sources and the wrong address in ChatGPT may be a right address in Perplexity, with different sources behind each.
Step two: fix the fact at every source you control
Your website first: the true fact stated plainly on the page a buyer would land on, in the form the question is asked, with schema that agrees with the visible text, per the schema guide. Then your profiles and listings, the same fact, the same wording, everywhere the business is described. Then the sources you do not control: the directory that takes corrections, the article's author, the platform's claim-and-correct process. Work the list in the order the answers cite them. A citation shown in the answer is the engine telling you which source it believed; fix that one first.
Step three: outvote the sources you cannot fix
Some sources never change: the archived article, the dead directory, the review from 2019. Corroboration is a vote, and a fact stated consistently by your site, your profiles, and your current listings outweighs a stale source the way three witnesses outweigh one. The entity work in the entity SEO guide is the standing version of this step: one set of facts, stated identically in every place the engines read, until the wrong version is the minority report in its own record. What does not work is stating the true fact in one place and leaving five stale statements standing. The engine is not choosing which version it likes. It is reporting which version it could verify most often.
How long until the answer changes?
Retrieved facts move at crawl speed: days to a few weeks after the sources are fixed and re-crawled, varying by engine and by how often the source is visited. Perplexity and Google's AI answers, built close to live indexes, usually move first. Facts an engine repeats from model memory move at retraining speed, which is measured in months and is not schedulable by anyone outside the company that trains the model. The practical discipline is the re-test: the same questions, the same engines, on a monthly cadence, with the answers recorded against the original error, until the correction holds across runs. That cadence is what the AI Presence, Measured service runs for clients who would rather read the report than run the questions.
Frequently asked questions
Can I contact ChatGPT or Google and ask them to correct an answer?
There is no correction desk that edits answers about a business, and feedback buttons on an answer report the response without changing your record. The answers are assembled from sources, so the correction has to happen at the sources: your site, your profiles, your listings, and the pages the answer cites. Fix those, and the answer follows at crawl speed.
Why does the AI answer still show my old address?
Because the old address is still stated somewhere the engine reads: a stale listing, a directory that scraped it years ago, an old page on your own site, or a profile you forgot existed. Search your business name with the old address and work through what you find. The version stated in the most places wins the answer, so every surviving copy has to be corrected or outvoted.
How do I stop wrong facts from coming back?
Keep one set of facts and maintain it as one document: when an address, a price, or a service changes, the change is made on the site, in the schema, in the llms.txt key facts, and on every profile in the same pass. Most wrong facts in AI answers are old truths that were corrected in one place and left standing in four others.
Does the AI Visibility Audit cover wrong facts?
Yes. The audit records what the answers say before it reads your site, so wrong facts surface as findings with the exact claim, the engine that made it, and the sources behind it, and the report's fix list is ordered so the corrections a buyer would hit first are repaired first. The audit is $750 flat and the report is yours to keep.
